before: An enum defines a value type with named integer constants. StudyState.Planned is a named value, not a quoted string. In this single-file program, put the enum type declaration after the executable top-level statements.
Without explicit numbers, enum members start at zero and increase by one. Compare values with ==. Printing a defined member shows its name.
An enum gives names, but numeric casts can still create values without a declared name. Do not treat an enum alone as validation of outside input.
Expected behavior from this example: Planned. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer task: Add a Paused member and test a separate branch for it; keep unexpected numeric values in mind. Use a .NET 10 console project with C# 14; reading completion does not verify this local work.
after: An enum is a type with named number values. StudyState gives names to three study stages: Planned, Active, and Done.
StudyState.Planned is a named value, not text in quotes. Unless you supply numbers, enum members start at zero and increase by one.
The == operator checks whether two enum values are equal. This program checks whether the current state is Done.
The program prints Planned. The state is not Done, so the else branch prints the enum value's name.
Converting a number to an enum can create a value with no declared name. Check input from outside the program; an enum's names alone do not guarantee that the value is allowed.
